chapters.intro: The building blocks you use every single day: counting, telling the time, and the days, months and dates. Tap 🔊 to hear each one in a natural voice.

sections.title: 21–99: eenheid eerst
sections.note: Say the unit first, then 'en', then the ten: vijfentwintig = 5‑and‑20 (25).

sections.title: Big numbers & money
sections.body: honderd = 100, duizend = 1.000, een miljoen = 1,000,000. Dutch uses a dot for thousands and a comma for decimals: € 3,50 is 'drie euro vijftig'.

sections.title: Rangtelwoorden (1e, 2e, 3e …)
sections.note: Use 'de' + the ordinal: de eerste, de tweede. 2nd–7th add ‑de, then mostly ‑ste.

sections.title: De dagen van de week
sections.note: Days are written lowercase in Dutch — no capital letter.

sections.title: Hoe laat is het? (the clock)
sections.note: Watch out: 'half drie' = 2:30 (half TO three), not 3:30. kwart over = quarter past, kwart voor = quarter to.

items.nl: Het is vijf voor half acht.
Het is vijf over half negen.
Mijn verjaardag is op twaalf maart.

chapters.intro: The small words that hold every sentence together: who is doing what (I, you, he…), whose something is (my, your…), and the famous de / het / een.

sections.title: u or jij?
sections.body: Use 'u' (formal) with strangers, officials, older people and often at work. Use 'jij/je' (informal) with friends, family and children. At an appointment or a counter, it's safest to start with 'u'.

sections.title: Aanwijzend — this / that
sections.note: deze/die go with de‑words, dit/dat go with het‑words.

sections.title: Articles: de, het, een
sections.body: Every noun is a 'de‑word' or a 'het‑word'. de = the (about 2/3 of nouns, ALL plurals, and people); het = the (about 1/3, neuter); een = a/an. There's no reliable rule, so learn de/het together with each new noun. Handy: every diminutive (‑je) is a het‑word, e.g. het huisje.

chapters.intro: Where you're from, the languages you speak, and how to say it. In Dutch, countries, languages and nationalities all start with a capital letter.

sections.title: Nationaliteiten
sections.note: Many have a male and female form: Nederlander (m) / Nederlandse (f).

items.nl: Ik spreek Turks, Engels en een beetje Nederlands.
items.en: I speak Turkish, English and a little Dutch.

chapters.intro: How Dutch verbs change for the present, the past and the future — plus the word‑order rules that trip everyone up. Master the present and the perfect tense first; together they cover most daily conversation.

sections.title: Present tense (tegenwoordige tijd)
sections.body: Take the stem (infinitive minus ‑en). ik = stem; jij/u/hij/zij = stem + t; wij/jullie/zij = the full infinitive. With werken (stem 'werk'): ik werk, jij werkt, wij werken.

sections.title: Perfect tense (voltooid t.t.) — the everyday past
sections.body: To talk about the past, Dutch usually uses hebben/zijn + a past participle (often ge‑…‑t / ‑d / ‑en). Use 'zijn' for movement or a change of state (gaan, komen, worden); otherwise 'hebben'. The participle goes to the END.

sections.title: Simple past (onvoltooid verleden tijd)
sections.body: Used for stories and descriptions. Regular verbs add ‑te(n)/‑de(n): werken → werkte, wonen → woonde. Common verbs are irregular: zijn → was/waren, hebben → had, gaan → ging. For everyday speaking you can lean on the perfect tense above.

sections.title: Future (toekomst)
sections.body: Easiest: gaan + infinitive for plans — 'Ik ga morgen werken' (I'm going to work tomorrow). Use 'zullen' for promises/offers — 'Ik zal het doen' (I'll do it). Dutch also often just uses the present with a time word: 'Morgen werk ik'.

sections.title: Modal verbs (kunnen, mogen, moeten, willen, zullen)
sections.body: These helper verbs send the main verb (an infinitive) to the END of the sentence: 'Ik wil naar huis gaan' (I want to go home).

sections.title: Word order (the big one)
sections.body: In a main sentence the verb is ALWAYS the second idea (V2). If you start with something else (e.g. a time), the subject moves after the verb: 'Morgen ga ik…'. Order of the rest: Time – Manner – Place. In a sub‑clause (omdat, dat, als…) the verb jumps to the END.

items.nl: Ik ga morgen naar de stad.
items.en: I'm going to the city tomorrow.

items.nl: Morgen ga ik naar de stad.
items.en: Tomorrow I'm going to the city.

items.nl: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
items.en: I'm staying home because I'm ill.

items.nl: Hij zegt dat hij geen tijd heeft.
items.en: He says he has no time.

chapters.intro: A toolbox of small but essential rules — asking questions, saying 'not / no', making plurals, and being polite — that you'll use in almost every conversation.

sections.title: niet or geen?
sections.body: Use 'geen' before a noun with no article or 'een': 'Ik heb geen tijd' (I have no time). Use 'niet' for everything else — verbs, adjectives, the rest: 'Ik werk niet vandaag' (I'm not working today).

sections.title: Plural (meervoud)
sections.body: Most nouns add ‑en (boek → boeken, huis → huizen). Words ending in ‑el, ‑em, ‑en, ‑er or a vowel usually add ‑s (tafel → tafels, appel → appels). A few add ‑'s after a/o/u/i/y (foto → foto's, baby → baby's).

sections.title: Verkleinwoord: ‑je (diminutive)
sections.body: Add ‑je (or ‑tje/‑pje/‑etje) to make something small, cute or casual — very common in Dutch. 'een kopje koffie' = a (little) cup of coffee. Diminutives are ALWAYS het‑words.

sections.title: Adjectives: add ‑e
sections.body: Before a noun, an adjective usually takes ‑e: de grote man, de mooie stad, een leuke film. Exception: a het‑word with 'een' takes NO ‑e — 'een groot huis', 'een klein kind'.

sections.title: Separable verbs (opbellen, meenemen…)
sections.body: Many verbs split in a main sentence — the prefix jumps to the end. opbellen → 'Ik bel je op' (I'll call you). meenemen → 'Ik neem het mee' (I'll take it). aankomen → 'De trein komt aan'.

items.nl: Hoe zeg je ... in het Nederlands?
items.en: How do you say ... in Dutch?

chapters.intro: KNM = 40 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes about how life in the Netherlands works. You watch short scenes and photos and pick the best answer. It's one of the easiest parts to pass early, so many people sit it first.

items.label: ▶ Oefen KNM in de app (met timer)

sections.title: Wat wordt er getoetst?
sections.body: Practical knowledge about Dutch society: work & income, education, health & care, housing, history & geography, government & the rule of law, official bodies (instanties), and norms & values. You don't memorise dates — you need to know how things work and what's normal here.

sections.title: Geschiedenis & geografie — kernfeiten
sections.note: Facts that come up a lot.

items.nl: De regering zit in Den Haag.
items.en: The government is in The Hague.

items.nl: de Deltawerken beschermen tegen het water
items.en: the Delta Works protect against the water
Much land lies below sea level.

items.nl: de Tweede Kamer en de Eerste Kamer
items.en: the House of Representatives & the Senate

items.nl: We kiezen de regering bij verkiezingen.
items.en: We elect the government in elections.

items.nl: Iedereen is gelijk voor de wet.
items.en: Everyone is equal before the law.

items.nl: De huisarts is je eerste contact.
items.en: The GP is your first point of contact.
The municipality arranges a lot locally.
A deal is a deal (be reliable).

sections.q: Wie is het staatshoofd van Nederland?
sections.qEn: Who is the head of state of the Netherlands?
sections.explanation: The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy: the King (Willem-Alexander) is head of state, while the prime minister leads the government.

sections.qEn: How many provinces does the Netherlands have?

sections.q: Je bent ziek en hebt een dokter nodig. Wat doe je eerst?
sections.qEn: You're ill and need a doctor. What do you do first?
sections.explanation: Your huisarts (GP) is the first point of contact and refers you to a hospital or specialist if needed.

sections.title: Tip
sections.body: Sit KNM early — it's very bankable. Practise with the free official KNM environment and the 450+ questions on KNM Oefenen (both in the Bronnen list under Oefenen).

chapters.intro: The Reading exam: about 65 minutes on a computer. You read everyday texts — letters, ads, signs, short articles — and answer multiple-choice questions.

items.label: ▶ Oefen Lezen in de app (met timer)

sections.title: Hoe werkt het?
sections.body: You get several short texts, each with a few multiple-choice questions. You can go back, change answers, and flag questions to return to. You don't need to understand every word — just enough to answer.

sections.title: Tips & hints
sections.body: 1) Read the QUESTION first, then scan the text for that information. 2) Watch out for negation — niet / geen flips the meaning. 3) Notice signal words (maar, want, omdat, daarom). 4) Manage your time; don't get stuck on one question.

sections.q: De bibliotheek is open van dinsdag tot en met zaterdag. Op maandag en zondag is de bibliotheek gesloten.
sections.qEn: Text: 'The library is open Tuesday to Saturday. On Monday and Sunday it's closed.' — On which day is the library open?
sections.explanation: 'Van dinsdag tot en met zaterdag' = Tuesday through Saturday, so Wednesday is open; Monday and Sunday are closed.

sections.title: Tip
sections.body: Read easy Dutch every day — Wablieft and NOS Jeugdjournaal (in Bronnen) — and do the official DUO reading practice for the real format.

chapters.intro: The Listening exam: about 45 minutes on a computer with headphones. You hear short conversations and announcements and answer multiple-choice questions.

items.label: ▶ Oefen Luisteren in de app (met timer)

sections.title: Hoe werkt het?
sections.body: You usually hear each fragment twice. Read the question and the options BEFORE the audio starts, so you know exactly what to listen for.

sections.title: Tips & hints
sections.body: 1) Listen for the key facts: who, where, when, how much, what time. 2) Don't panic if you miss a word — focus on the overall meaning. 3) Use the second listen to check your answer.

sections.q: De trein naar Amsterdam van tien voor drie vertrekt vandaag van spoor vijf, niet van spoor twee.
sections.qEn: Announcement (tap 🔊): 'The 2:50 train to Amsterdam leaves from platform 5 today, not platform 2.' — Which platform does the train leave from?
sections.explanation: Listen for the correction: 'van spoor vijf, niet van spoor twee'. The answer is platform 5.

sections.title: Tip
sections.body: The official DUO listening practice uses real exam audio — use it. Podcasts like 'Een Beetje Nederlands' (in Bronnen) train your ear with slow, clear Dutch.

chapters.intro: The Writing exam: about 40 minutes, on paper. You write short, practical texts — fill in a form, write a brief note or email, and answer questions.

sections.title: Hoe werkt het?
sections.body: Tasks are everyday and short: complete a form with your details, write a brief message (to a teacher, neighbour or company), or answer a few written questions. Neat, simple, correct sentences score well.

sections.title: Tips & hints
sections.body: 1) Answer EVERY part of the task. 2) Keep sentences short and check word order (verb second). 3) Use a greeting and a sign-off in messages. 4) Re-read for de/het, spelling, and verb endings (don't forget the -t!).

sections.q: Schrijf een kort bericht aan je buurvrouw. Je gaat op vakantie. Vraag of zij je planten water wil geven.
sections.qEn: Task: Write a short message to your neighbour. You're going on holiday. Ask if she'll water your plants.
sections.answer:
Beste Anke,

Ik ga twee weken op vakantie, van 1 tot 14 juli. Wil je alsjeblieft mijn planten water geven? De sleutel ligt bij mijn zus om de hoek. Alvast bedankt!

Met vriendelijke groet,
Mert
sections.explanation: Notice the parts: a greeting, the situation, a clear request, one practical detail, and a sign-off. That's all an A2 task needs.

sections.title: Tip
sections.body: Memorise 3–4 templates (a request, a complaint, a cancellation, filling in a form) and write a few lines every day. The lessons in each Thema have a writing exercise with a model answer.

chapters.intro: The Speaking exam: about 35 minutes on a computer. You speak into a microphone — describe a photo, answer questions, and react to short video situations.

sections.title: Hoe werkt het?
sections.body: You see or hear a prompt, get a few seconds to think, then record your spoken answer. There's no live examiner — the computer records you. Understandable beats perfect.

sections.title: Tips & hints
sections.body: 1) Speak in short, clear sentences. 2) Use phrases you already know. 3) Need a moment? Say 'Eh, even denken...'. 4) Answer the whole question, with one example or detail.

items.nl: Ik ben het er niet mee eens.

sections.q: Je ziet een foto van een man in de supermarkt. Beschrijf wat je ziet.
sections.qEn: Task: You see a photo of a man in the supermarket. Describe what you see.
sections.answer: Op de foto zie ik een man in de supermarkt. Hij doet boodschappen. Hij heeft brood en melk in zijn mandje. Hij staat bij de kassa en betaalt.
sections.explanation: Cover who, where, what they're doing, and a detail — 3–4 simple sentences is plenty at A2.

sections.title: Tip
sections.body: Rehearse with the Gesprekken tab (read the yellow lines out loud) and do the official DUO speaking practice to see the real format.
